summary: After the Gutian interlude, Ur-Nammu of Ur (r. c. 2112–2094 BCE) reunited Sumer and Akkad, and his son Shulgi built a centralised, bureaucratic state of some twenty provinces ringed by a military periphery along the Zagros. Amorite incursions, revolts and the breakaway of Isin weakened his successors, and c. 2004 BCE an Elamite coalition sacked Ur. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.
details: After Akkad fell, Sumer was split between Gutian rulers and revived city-states, until Utu-hengal of Uruk defeated the Gutian king Tirigan. Ur-Nammu, who had governed Ur and may have been Utu-hengal's brother, then took power himself c. 2112 BCE, defeated his former masters at Uruk and conquered Lagash. Taking the title 'King of Sumer and Akkad', he reunited southern Mesopotamia, restored temples and canals, and began the Great Ziggurat of Ur. The oldest surviving law collection, the Code of Ur-Nammu, is linked to him or his son. Sumer was once again a single kingdom, now ruled from Ur.

Ur-Nammu pushed his rule north-east towards the Diyala valley, probably defeating the Elamite king Puzur-Inshushinak along the way. After about 18 years on the throne he died on the battlefield in the eastern highlands; a later poem, the 'Death of Ur-Nammu', mourns him, and some read it as saying his army abandoned him. His son Shulgi succeeded c. 2094 BCE and reigned for about 48 years, roughly half the life of the whole dynasty. Shulgi would turn his father's kingdom into an empire on the model of Akkad, although his first twenty years are known mostly from temple-building.

Around the middle of his reign Shulgi carried out reforms that reshaped the state, though some may have begun under his father and few can be dated exactly. He reorganised the army, standardised weights and measures, reformed writing and the scribal schools, and unified taxes, including the bala system in which each province took turns supplying the centre. A huge livestock and administrative hub was built at Puzrish-Dagan near Nippur. By his 21st year, and perhaps as early as his 12th, Shulgi had proclaimed himself a god. The result looked like a highly centralised state, at least in its Sumerian core.

Shulgi's later reign was dominated by wars in the Zagros foothills and along the upper Tigris, lands rich in pasture and trade routes. His 25th year-name records the destruction of Simurrum, a mountain kingdom north of the Diyala; later names boast of destroying it a second, a third and eventually a ninth time, showing how hard such enemies were to hold down. Conquered districts became a defensive, tribute-paying periphery with garrisons and military colonies, rather like the Roman frontier. On the map, Ur's power now reached north-east from Sumer towards the Zagros.

Alongside war, Shulgi used marriage diplomacy with the kingdoms of the Iranian plateau. In his 18th year a daughter became queen of Marhashi, and the name for his 30th year records that the governor of Anshan, in Elam, married another daughter; others married rulers of Pashime. Such ties did not guarantee peace: by his 34th year Shulgi was campaigning against Anshan, and a year-name records its destruction. The kings of Ur also controlled Susa, where Shulgi built temples, so Elam's western lowlands were drawn firmly into Ur's orbit.

Amorites (Martu), Semitic-speaking groups from Syria and Upper Mesopotamia often described as tribal and nomadic, had been moving into southern Mesopotamia since late Akkadian times. In his 37th year Shulgi built 'the wall of the land' in the north of Akkad to keep out the Tidnum, an Amorite group. The wall marked the empire's north-western frontier and showed that pressure from the steppe had become a lasting worry. His successors had to reinforce it, and Amorite incursions eventually played a major part in the empire's collapse.

The climax of Shulgi's wars came near the end of his reign. The name for his 45th year boasts that he 'smashed the heads of Urbilum, Simurrum, Lullubum and Karhar in a single campaign'. Urbilum is Arbela (modern Erbil in northern Iraq), and the other lands lay in the Zagros foothills; around the same time he destroyed Kimash and Hurtum near Elam. These victories pushed Ur's ring of tribute-paying border lands to its widest, stretching along the Tigris and the Zagros from Urbilum to Susa, and made Ur the leading power of Mesopotamia.

After Shulgi died, his son Amar-Sin reigned about nine years, followed by Amar-Sin's brother Shu-Sin (c. 2037–2029 BCE). Shu-Sin had to reassert control in the northern and eastern borderlands, where tribute was arriving less regularly, a sign that Ur's grip was loosening. The most threatening danger came from Amorites in the north-west, and after an open revolt he built a new fortified wall between the Euphrates and the Tigris, strengthening Shulgi's defences. Late in his reign much real power lay with his chancellor Aradmu. The borders held for now, but the outer lands were slipping.

Ibbi-Sin, probably Shu-Sin's son, came to the throne c. 2028 BCE and reigned for 24 years while the empire fell apart. The archives of the main administrative centres in the heartland dry up after his third year, a sign that the central bureaucracy had lost control of the provinces. Eastern lands such as Anshan and Susa broke away, Eshnunna became independent, and Amorite raids grew more violent. In his seventh and eighth years the price of grain rose to some 60 times normal, pointing to famine. On the map, Ur's empire shrank towards the city of Ur itself.

Ishbi-Erra, an official described as a 'man of Mari', had been sent by Ibbi-Sin to buy grain at Isin and Kazallu. According to letters preserved as later school exercises, whose authenticity is uncertain, he complained that Amorite raids stopped him shipping it and asked to be made governor of Isin and Nippur. By Ibbi-Sin's eighth year he was dating documents by his own year-names, in effect declaring independence at Isin. His power grew as Ibbi-Sin's declined, splitting the former empire in two, and his dynasty of Isin would later present itself as Ur's heir.

By the end Ibbi-Sin held little beyond the city of Ur. Around 2004 BCE (middle chronology) an army from Elam and the Shimashki highlands of the Zagros, led by King Kindattu, sacked Ur and carried Ibbi-Sin off in chains to Elam, where he died. The disaster was remembered in the 'Lament for Sumer and Ur', which describes the city reduced to ruin mounds. The Elamites occupied Ur until Ishbi-Erra of Isin drove them out. The fall of Ur ended the last great Sumerian state, and Mesopotamia split into rival Amorite-led kingdoms such as Isin and Larsa.
